papers.full_citation: Chaudhry, G. I., et al. (2026). Murakkab: Resource-Efficient Agentic Workflow Orchestration in Cloud Platforms. OSDI '26.
papers.summary: Declarative workflow compiled to a DAG; a Profile-Guided Optimizer (MILP) jointly assigns model, hardware, and parallelism per task, solved once per workflow instance, using real profiled cost/latency/reliability data rather than assumptions.

full_detail.problem: [RECONSTRUCTED FROM PRIOR-SESSION SUMMARY, NOT RE-DERIVED FROM THE ORIGINAL PDF] Existing agentic workflow systems fix model/hardware assignment at design time or make per-call decisions without a holistic, whole-DAG view, leading to inefficient resource use in cloud deployment of multi-step agentic workflows.
full_detail.method: Declarative workflow specification compiled into a DAG. A Profile-Guided Optimizer inspects the full DAG before execution and solves a MILP that jointly assigns model + hardware/resource + parallelism configuration per task, using profiled (measured, not assumed) cost/latency/reliability data. Decision is made once per workflow instance, not per call.
full_detail.results: [Not re-derivable without the source PDF — original session's extracted numbers are not preserved in the handoff summary.]
full_detail.limitations: MILP requires a specialized/licensed solver (CPLEX/Gurobi/GLPK-class), does not adapt to drift without a full re-solve, and is heavyweight relative to the compute/engineering budget of a one-semester student project.

concept_links.detail: Murakkab is the origin of the whole-DAG-before-assignment framing this project adopts.
Origin of the Profile-Guided Optimization concept: real measured data, not assumptions, drives allocation.
Murakkab's optimizer core is a MILP; this project explicitly replaces it with a heuristic while keeping MILP as an optional offline baseline.

papers.full_citation: Hua, W., Karne, S., Xie, Q., Agrawal, A., Pagonas, N., Kaffes, K., & Peng, T. (2026). AgentOpt v0.1 Technical Report: Client-Side Optimization for LLM-Based Agent. arXiv:2604.06296v2.
papers.role_label: Client-side model-combination selection framework; strong conceptual and evaluation-methodology overlap with S1/S2, direct precedent for treating model assignment as a combinatorial search problem
papers.summary: Introduces AGENTOPT, a framework-agnostic Python package for client-side optimization of multi-step agent pipelines, focused first on model-combination selection: given a pipeline with multiple roles and a candidate model pool per role, find the cost-effective model-to-role assignment via black-box combinatorial search (ten algorithms, notably Matrix UCB-E), rather than per-call routing. Central empirical finding: best combination does not equal the combination of best individual models — role interactions dominate, with 13-32x cost gaps between combinations at matched accuracy, and Matrix UCB-E recovering near-optimal accuracy at 62-76% less evaluation cost than brute force.

full_detail.problem: Existing agent-efficiency research is almost entirely server-side (caching, speculative execution, scheduling, load balancing), optimizing shared provider infrastructure. But developers building agent pipelines from heterogeneous models, tools, and APIs face a distinct client-side problem: how to allocate model choice, local tools, and API budget across pipeline stages/roles, subject to application-specific quality-cost-latency constraints that only the developer (not the provider) knows. Within client-side optimization, model selection is argued to be the dominant lever because it is upstream of every other optimization (caching/scheduling only matter after models are fixed), and because model quality is role-dependent, not a context-free property of the model in isolation — so the optimization unit must be the full model combination across all pipeline roles, evaluated end-to-end, not per-call routing of individual queries.
full_detail.method: Formalizes a pipeline with H roles and candidate model set(s) M_i per role; a 'combo' c = (m1,...,mH) is one full assignment. Executing combo c on the dataset induces trajectory tau(c) with measured PERF, LATENCY, COST; utility J(c) = U(PERF, LATENCY, COST), goal c* = argmax J(c) over the combinatorial space C = product of M_i (size can be exponential in number of roles). This is framed as a black-box / pure-exploration multi-armed-bandit problem: each combo is an arm, pulling it means evaluating on one datapoint. AGENTOPT implements ten search algorithms to explore this space sample-efficiently: Brute-force, Random search, Matrix UCB-E (treats the combo-by-datapoint grid as a matrix, UCB score = mean + sqrt(a/n), batches evaluation toward highest-UCB combo), Matrix UCB-E-LRF (adds a low-rank factorization ensemble to predict unobserved grid cells and target high-uncertainty cells), Arm Elimination (default method; rounds of evaluation with elimination of combos whose upper bound falls below current leader's lower bound), Epsilon-LUCB (targets epsilon-optimal best-arm ID via leader/challenger sampling), Threshold Successive Elimination (finds all combos above a quality threshold rather than the single best), Hill Climbing (local search over a role-by-role neighborhood, multiple random restarts), Bayesian Optimization (surrogate model + acquisition function, via BoTorch), and LM Proposal (uses an LLM to propose promising combos before empirical evaluation, without exhaustive search). Systems-wise, AGENTOPT is framework-agnostic: it intercepts LLM calls at the HTTP transport layer (patching httpx.Client.send / AsyncClient.send) and uses Python contextvars to attribute each call to the current datapoint and combo, requiring no changes to agent code. It includes HTTP-level response caching (keyed by request-payload hash, persisted to SQLite, preserving original latency even on cache hits) and a two-level semaphore for bounded parallel evaluation (across combos and across datapoints within a combo). Output is a ranked SelectionResults object with a Pareto frontier over accuracy/cost/latency, exportable to CSV/YAML.
full_detail.results: Evaluated on 9 models via AWS Bedrock (Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude 3 Haiku, gpt-oss-120b, gpt-oss-20b, Kimi K2.5, Qwen3 Next 80B A3B, Qwen3 32B, Ministral 3 8B) across four benchmarks: HotpotQA (199 examples, 2-role planner-solver, 81 combos), GPQA Diamond (198 examples, single-role, 9 combos), MathQA (200 examples, 2-role answerer-critic, 81 combos), BFCL v3 Multi-Turn (200 examples, single-role, 9 combos). Central finding: at matched accuracy, cost gap between best and worst model combinations ranges 13-32x across benchmarks (e.g. on BFCL, Qwen3 Next 80B matches Claude Opus 4.6 accuracy at 32x lower cost). On HotpotQA, Claude Opus 4.6 (the strongest standalone model) is the worst planner across all 81 combinations because it tends to answer directly and bypass the solver's search tools; the best combo pairs the cheapest planner (Ministral 3 8B) with Opus as solver, reaching 74.27% accuracy vs only 31.71% when Opus is used for both roles. On algorithm comparison (50-seed averages): Matrix UCB-E is the strongest selector overall, recovering near-optimal accuracy while observing only ~20% of the evaluation grid, giving 62-76% cost savings vs brute force (e.g. HotpotQA: 73.54% mean acc at budget 0.2 vs 74.27% ground truth, using 3,234 evals vs 16,168 for brute force). Matrix UCB-E-LRF underperforms plain Matrix UCB-E despite its added complexity. Arm Elimination and Hill Climbing perform comparably on average (78.9% vs 79.1% mean accuracy across benchmarks) but Hill Climbing is sensitive to search-space topology (100% find rate on BFCL/GPQA, drops to 52% find rate on HotpotQA where the optimum is counterintuitive). LM Proposal (using an LLM's priors to propose combos) works only when raw capability predicts performance (GPQA) and fails badly where role interactions are non-obvious (HotpotQA, BFCL).
full_detail.limitations: Framed as a v0.1 technical report; model selection is presented as only the 'first functionality' of a broader intended client-side optimization package (future work explicitly includes adaptive routing, tool selection, scheduling, personalized utility-aware policies). Evaluation is limited to text/tool-use benchmarks with 2-role pipelines at most (no evidence yet for deeper/longer DAGs). Brute-force ground truth itself is nontrivial in cost even for 2-role, moderate-size pipelines (up to ~$124 for MathQA's 81-combo grid), which is the same tractability problem this project's own heuristic approach is designed to sidestep, but AGENTOPT addresses it via sample-efficient *search* over a fixed, whole-DAG-known set of combos rather than a *drift-adaptive, single-pass* heuristic scoring walk — a different design point from this project's DAG-walking allocator.

concept_links.detail: AgentOpt's central contribution: treating a full model-to-role assignment across the whole pipeline (not a per-call routing decision) as the atomic unit of optimization — directly analogous to this project's own move of assigning model+hardware+config once per whole DAG rather than per task in isolation.

AgentOpt's pipeline-with-roles formulation is structurally similar to a DAG of tasks, though the paper treats pipelines somewhat more loosely (roles in sequence/interaction) than this project's explicit topological-DAG execution model; still directly supports the 'decide once per whole workflow, not per call' framing this project uses.

AgentOpt's bandit/heuristic search algorithms (Arm Elimination, Matrix UCB-E, Hill Climbing) are a different flavor of 'avoid exact/exhaustive solving' than this project's single-pass topological scoring heuristic, but share the same underlying motivation: exact/exhaustive evaluation over the full assignment space is too costly, so a cheaper approximate method is substituted.

papers.caveats: AgentOpt's core mechanism (search over a fixed model-combination space using a labeled evaluation dataset, selecting once via bandit/local-search before deployment) is a different design point from this project's drift-correcting, single-pass, per-execution heuristic allocator — flag as a scope difference, not equivalence, when citing. Best framed as (a) strong support for the 'assign per whole pipeline, not per call, because role interactions dominate' argument (supports C_COMBO_SELECTION / C_DAG), and (b) a source of reusable systems engineering patterns (HTTP transport-layer interception, Pareto-frontier evaluation reporting) rather than as a source for the drift-correction or DAG-topological-walk mechanisms themselves. Given the project's identified structural gap (S1 is thin, only C_DAG), this paper's combo/pipeline framing is a reasonable, if partial, contribution to S1 as well as S2 — worth flagging to the user given the standing instruction to prioritize S1-strengthening papers.

papers.full_citation: Bruinaars, P. (2025). A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach to Prescriptive Process Monitoring. MSc Thesis, Utrecht University. Supervisors: X. Lu, S. Wang.
papers.role_label: Adjacent-domain precedent for decentralized, agent-per-resource task allocation under partial observability; strong methodological parallel for S1 (workflow/task execution modeling) and S3 (baseline-driven evaluation), different mechanism (learned RL policy vs. profile-guided heuristic scoring) for S2
papers.summary: Presents MASTER, a Dec-POMDP-based multi-agent simulation environment for Business Process Optimization / Prescriptive Process Monitoring, where each resource (human or machine) executing tasks in a business process is modeled as an autonomous agent with partial observability, learning (via MAPPO or QMIX) when to volunteer for upcoming tasks from an event-log-driven task stream. Evaluated on three real/semi-synthetic datasets (CVS Pharmacy, Loan application, BPI12W) against three baselines (random, best-median, ground-truth), using throughput/waiting/processing time as metrics with non-parametric statistical testing (Kruskal-Wallis, Mann-Whitney U with Bonferroni, Cliff's delta). Results are mixed and dataset-dependent: QMIX generally outperforms MAPPO, MAPPO does best on CVS, QMIX on BPI12W, and both struggle on the loan-application dataset — no MARL approach uniformly beats the simple ground-truth/random baselines.

full_detail.problem: Existing RL approaches to Business Process Optimization (BPO) and Prescriptive Process Monitoring (PPM) assume a single centralized agent with full visibility over the process and its resources, which is unrealistic for real, distributed processes where many human/automated actors act with only local, partial information and must coordinate implicitly. No prior work had systematically applied Multi-Agent RL (MARL), modeling each resource as its own decision-making agent, to PPM/BPO using real event-log data.
full_detail.method: Models the business process environment as a Dec-POMDP: each resource (employee/machine) that can execute activities is an autonomous agent with a fixed set of capabilities (activities it can perform, with per-activity historical performance PDFs), a task queue, and a learned policy — no explicit 'type' or fixed schedule (simplified relative to the related AgentSimulator work). At each timestep, an upcoming task arrives from a stream (derived from the process's event log); agents each choose a binary action ('volunteer' or not) based on a partial observation (upcoming task identity, their own historical performance stats on that task type, current queue length, remaining duration of their current task, and capability flag for the upcoming task). If multiple agents volunteer, one is picked at random among capable volunteers; if none volunteer, one is picked at random among all capable agents. The task is added to the winning agent's FIFO queue. Reward is simply the negative throughput time of each task as it completes (f(d) = -d, d = completion_time - assigned_time), a deliberately simple, dataset-agnostic reward. Two MARL algorithms are trained on top of this environment: MAPPO (multi-agent PPO, on-policy, actor-critic with centralized-training-decentralized-execution/CTDE, clipped surrogate objective) and QMIX (value-based, off-policy, CTDE, per-agent Q-functions combined via a monotonic mixing network into a global Q-value, avoiding the exponential blow-up of the joint action space). The environment is implemented as a parallel PettingZoo environment (rebuilt from scratch rather than reusing the prior AgentSimulator/Mesa codebase, since Mesa isn't designed for MARL). Training is fully offline (80/20 train/test split on whole days of event-log data, non-overlapping start times), organized into training blocks (one full simulation pass per block, buffered and used to update policies over several epochs). Evaluation compares the resulting throughput/waiting/processing-time distributions against three baselines — random assignment, best-median-performer assignment, and ground-truth (as-logged) assignment — using Kolmogorov-Smirnov normality tests (which reliably fail, given heavy-tailed event-log data), Kruskal-Wallis H-tests for overall significance, and pairwise Mann-Whitney U-tests with Bonferroni correction plus Cliff's delta effect sizes.
full_detail.results: On the CVS Pharmacy dataset (6 resources, 15 activities, 10,000 traces): MAPPO gives a slight but statistically significant improvement in median throughput time over ground truth (driven by processing time, at a small cost in waiting time); QMIX performs statistically indistinguishable from random/ground-truth baselines but significantly beats the best-median baseline. On the Loan application dataset (19 resources, 12 activities, 1,000 traces): both MAPPO and QMIX perform worse than ground truth and random baselines on most metrics (though both beat the poor best-median baseline by a large margin) — the paper attributes this to long task durations combined with the one-task-per-agent-at-a-time assumption. On BPI12W (52 resources, 6 activities, 8,616 traces, real-world event log): QMIX is the best performer overall, beating all baselines and MAPPO on throughput and waiting time with small-to-large effect sizes, achieving a median throughput time over an hour faster than the next-best (ground-truth) baseline; MAPPO improves processing time but has worse waiting time than ground truth/random, netting a worse median throughput. Overall: QMIX generally outperforms MAPPO across datasets, but MAPPO wins on CVS specifically, so the thesis concludes there isn't enough evidence that one algorithm dominates the other; performance is highly dataset-dependent (interacting with number of resources, number of unique activities, and volume of training data).
full_detail.limitations: Explicitly exploratory/first-of-its-kind work: no formal hyperparameter tuning was performed (fixed hyperparameters chosen from preliminary experimentation, not grid search or Bayesian optimization); the simplified environment assumes each agent can work on only one task at a time and each case has only one active task/agent at a time, which the thesis itself flags as likely responsible for the poor loan-application results; the reward function (simple negative-throughput-time) is acknowledged as possibly numerically unstable and not necessarily optimal; conflict resolution when multiple/no agents volunteer is fully random, which the author suggests may be actively hurting performance and could be improved via inter-agent communication; results do not show a uniformly effective MARL approach — it sometimes underperforms even the trivial random-assignment baseline.
numbers: CVS: MAPPO median throughput 46.49 min vs ground-truth 47.85 min (small improvement); QMIX median throughput 47.85 min (~tied with ground truth)
CVS Kruskal-Wallis throughput: H=4808.18, epsilon^2=0.075, p<0.001
Loan application: MAPPO median throughput 3506.54 min vs ground-truth 2068.81 min (worse); best-median baseline median throughput 19437.93 min (far worse than all learned/other baselines)
BPI12W: QMIX median throughput 119.56 min vs ground-truth 182.69 min (QMIX more than an hour faster at the mean/tail level); best-median baseline catastrophic at 536366.57 min median throughput
Three datasets span 6/19/52 resources and 15/12/6 activity types (CVS/Loan/BPI12W), deliberately chosen to vary agent-count while keeping data volume workable for MARL training

concept_links.detail: Origin, in this map, of the Dec-POMDP framing: each resource/executor is modeled as an autonomous agent with only partial, local observability of the environment (its own queue, performance history, and the upcoming task), directly analogous to how this project's own DAG-executing profiled resources have only local/measured information rather than global omniscience.

Central mechanism of the paper: task-to-resource assignment is learned via trained RL policies (MAPPO/QMIX) rather than computed by a heuristic scoring function or solved via MILP. This is a genuinely different allocation mechanism than this project's profile-guided heuristic — useful as a contrast/alternative-design-space paper: it shows what a *learned* (not profiled/heuristic) allocation policy looks like for essentially the same class of problem (assign incoming tasks/work-items to capable resources under partial information to optimize throughput).

Each case is a sequence of tasks (a linear, not general-DAG, structure in this implementation), and the environment processes a stream of such sequences rather than a single whole-DAG-known-in-advance workflow — a looser structural analogy to this project's DAG model, worth noting as a scope difference: MASTER's agents decide per-task, online, without seeing the whole case's structure in advance, which is closer to per-call routing than this project's whole-DAG-before-assignment framing.

MASTER's agents continuously learn and adapt their volunteering policy from experience (via RL training), which is conceptually adjacent to this project's own drift-correction/self-updating profile idea, though the mechanism differs sharply: MASTER trains a neural policy via reward signal over many episodes, whereas this project's drift-correction is a lightweight exponential-moving-average nudge to a profiled estimate after each real execution, not a trained policy.

Provides a concrete, reusable evaluation template directly relevant to this project's own planned fault-injection evaluation: compare the proposed approach against multiple named baselines (here: random assignment, best-median/greedy-heuristic assignment, and ground-truth/as-logged assignment) using throughput/waiting/processing-time distributions, tested for significance with Kruskal-Wallis + Mann-Whitney U + Bonferroni correction and reported with Cliff's delta effect sizes rather than raw p-values alone — a rigorous, non-parametric-appropriate methodology given that real system/event-log timing data is reliably heavy-tailed and non-normal.

Uses throughput time, waiting time, and processing time as its core evaluation metrics — directly analogous to (and a validated precedent for) the cost/latency/reliability-style metrics this project's own evaluation plan intends to use, and demonstrates decomposing a single end-to-end time metric (throughput) into its waiting vs. processing components to diagnose *where* an allocation policy is winning or losing, a useful diagnostic pattern for this project's own fault-injection evaluation.

papers.caveats: Different application domain (human/machine resource allocation in classical business processes, e.g. pharmacy/loan-application workflows) rather than LLM-agent/model+hardware allocation, so it is not a directly citable technical precedent for this project's core Murakkab-derived mechanism. Its main value here is (a) a structurally similar decentralized, partial-observability, agent-per-resource framing that could strengthen the thin S1 (Workflow Orchestration) scope item, and (b) a rigorous, reusable non-parametric baseline-comparison evaluation methodology directly transferable to this project's own fault-injection evaluation plan (S3). Its central empirical finding — that a learned MARL policy does not uniformly beat simple baselines and is highly dataset-dependent — is also a useful cautionary data point when scoping expectations for this project's own heuristic allocator's evaluation. Recommend citing narrowly for the Dec-POMDP/partial-observability framing and the baseline+statistical-testing methodology, not for the allocation mechanism itself, which this project has already deliberately chosen not to pursue (learned RL policy vs. profile-guided heuristic scoring are different design points).
